top_choice_rationale: P001 (Helpman and Grossman, B001) has the cleanest attribution on the slate: a long, tightly coupled two-person programme, so nobody has to be arbitrarily excluded. The protection-for-sale framework turned lobbying and tariff formation into a tractable general-equilibrium object with sharp, falsifiable cross-sector predictions. It has shaped theory, estimation and the analysis of trade agreements for about three decades, so maturity is not in doubt. The main reservation is that empirical support for its specific predictions is mixed and specification-sensitive. I read that as a limit on the contribution, not a disqualification, and the citation should be confined to the political economy of trade protection without claiming empirical validation. The growth strand should stay out. I cannot verify the reported overlap with the 2025 prize, and it is not the discovery the ballot defines. I rank P002 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) second. The revised trio and narrower wording fix the attribution instability I raised earlier. The size, persistence and shift-share identification of the China-shock effects are still being revised, which argues for more time. P003 (Melitz, Helpman) is third. The firm-heterogeneity framework has been tested densely, but the credit gap around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be closed within three names, and it rests heavily on one 2003 paper. All three substantive proposals rank above no award (P000). I judge each a genuine achievement, with attribution and consolidation as the differences, and I did not weigh the number of supporters as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. My collaborators in matching, kidney exchange, refugee placement and school choice include none of Helpman, Grossman, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Melitz. My SSE affiliation alongside committee colleagues is not a tie to any candidate. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
